steps.label: String Handling
steps.content:
8.1 Programming Concepts

String Handling

Year 11

  • Today: count the characters in a string, take part of a string, and change it to capital or small letters.
  • Every time, ask why: why does it give that answer?
  • Activities: trace a program, then write your own string code and run it.
Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a program need to look at the characters inside a string?Show the answer

To check what the user typed: a password that is long enough, a code that starts with PD, a yes typed as YES or yes.

steps.label: LENGTH: Count the Characters
steps.content:
LENGTH: Count the Characters

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what does LENGTH("Happy Days") give? Why is it not 9?Show the worked answer

It gives 10.

The space is a character too. 5 letters, 1 space, 4 letters: 5 + 1 + 4 = 10.

Position12345678910
CharacterHappy·Days
CodeResult
LENGTH("Cat")3
LENGTH("Happy Days")10
LENGTH("Year 11")7
  • LENGTH(Word) gives the number of characters in Word.
  • Letters, digits, symbols and spaces all count.
  • The result is a whole number: an INTEGER.

steps.label: Check: LENGTH
steps.content:
Check: LENGTH

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is the result of LENGTH an INTEGER, not a STRING?Show the answer

LENGTH counts the characters. A count is a whole number.

Name holds "Ali Khan".

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Exam Question: Six Characters Long
steps.content:
Exam Question: Six Characters Long

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the rules in the question twice before you write code?Show the answer

Each rule becomes a test in your code. If you miss one word, your check is wrong.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/22, June 2024, Question 4(b)(i). A program needs to make sure the characters input for a product code meet these rules: the product code is six characters in length; the first two characters must be "PD"; the last four characters must be a number in the range 1000 to 9999 inclusive. The product code is stored in the variable Product.

items.prompt: Write the pseudocode to make sure that the product code is six characters in length.
items.modelAnswer:
IF LENGTH(Product) = 6 THEN
1 mark: LENGTH(Product). 1 mark: testing it against 6. A loop such as UNTIL LENGTH(Product) = 6 also gets both marks.

steps.label: SUBSTRING: Take Part of a String
steps.content:
SUBSTRING: Take Part of a String

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what does SUBSTRING("Computer", 1, 3) give? Why?Show the worked answer

It gives "Com".

1 is the start: the first character is position 1. 3 is how many characters to take: C, o, m.

Position12345678
CharacterComputer
CodeStartHow manyResult
SUBSTRING("Computer", 1, 3)13"Com"
SUBSTRING("Computer", 4, 3)43"put"
SUBSTRING("Computer", 8, 1)81"r"
  • SUBSTRING(Word, Start, Length): take Length characters, starting at position Start.
  • The first character is position 1.

steps.label: Compare: How Many, Not Where to Stop
steps.content:
Compare: How Many, Not Where to Stop

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does SUBSTRING("Computer", 3, 5) give "mpute" and not "mpu"?Show the answer

5 is how many characters to take, not the position to stop at.

Start at position 3, then take 5 characters: m, p, u, t, e.

Position12345678
CharacterComputer
CodeIf it meant "stop at"What SUBSTRING really gives
SUBSTRING("Computer", 3, 5)"mpu""mpute"
SUBSTRING("Computer", 2, 4)"omp""ompu"
  • The second value is where to start.
  • The third value is how many characters.

steps.label: Compare: Reaching the Last Character
steps.content:
Compare: Reaching the Last Character

Think → Pair → ShareBoth lines work for "Computer". Why does only the second line work for every word?Show the answer

8 is the last position only when the word has 8 characters. "Mouse" has no position 8, and in "Keyboards" position 8 is not the end.

LENGTH(Word) is always the position of the last character, whatever the word.

WordLENGTH(Word)SUBSTRING(Word, 8, 1)SUBSTRING(Word, LENGTH(Word), 1)
"Computer"8"r""r"
"Mouse"5Error: past the end"e"
"Keyboards"9"d""s"
  • The last character is at position LENGTH(Word).
  • A program must work for any word, not just the one you tested.

steps.content:
Check: SUBSTRING

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must a program never ask SUBSTRING for a position past the end?Show the answer

Every code has the same shape, so a wrong code can be found as soon as it is typed in.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/22, June 2024, Question 4(b)(ii). The same product code rules: six characters, the first two characters must be "PD", the last four characters a number from 1000 to 9999. The product code is stored in the variable Product.

items.prompt: Write the pseudocode to make sure that the first two characters of the product code are "PD".

The loop looks at one letter at a time. Each time round, Count moves on to the next position.

steps.label: UCASE and LCASE: Change the Case
steps.content:
UCASE and LCASE: Change the Case

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what does UCASE("Room 12b") give? Why do the 1 and the 2 not change?Show the worked answer

It gives "ROOM 12B".

UCASE changes small letters to capital letters. Digits and spaces have no capital, so they stay the same.

CodeResult
UCASE("Happy")"HAPPY"
LCASE("W")"w"
UCASE("Room 12b")"ROOM 12B"
LCASE("PD12")"pd12"
  • UCASE(Word) gives Word in upper case: capital letters.
  • LCASE(Word) gives Word in lower case: small letters.
  • Only letters change.

steps.label: Compare: "yes" and "YES"
steps.content:
Compare: "yes" and "YES"

Think → Pair → ShareThe user typed yes. Why does the first condition say No match?Show the answer

= checks every character exactly. A small y and a capital Y are different characters.

UCASE(Answer) turns yes, Yes and YES into YES first, so all three match.

Answer typedIF Answer = "YES" THENIF UCASE(Answer) = "YES" THEN
"YES"MatchMatch
"yes"No matchMatch
"Yes"No matchMatch
  • Users type in different ways.
  • Change the input to one case before you compare it.

steps.label: Compare: Store the Result
steps.content:
Compare: Store the Result

Think → Pair → SharePrograms A and B both use UCASE. Why do they still output sam?Show the answer

UCASE gives back a new string. It does not change Name.

A throws the new string away. B stores it in Big, not in Name. Only C stores it back in Name.

Name holds "sam".

ProgramLinesOutput
AUCASE(Name)
OUTPUT Name		sam: the new string is lost
BBig <- UCASE(Name)
OUTPUT Name		sam
CName <- UCASE(Name)
OUTPUT Name		SAM
  • A string function gives back a new value.
  • Store it with <-, or output it. On its own, it changes nothing.

steps.label: Check: UCASE and LCASE
steps.content:
Check: UCASE and LCASE

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does UCASE not change digits or spaces?Show the answer

Only letters have a capital and a small form. A digit or a space has only one form.

Capital letters matter.

Total: 4 marks

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/21, June 2023, Question 8(a). The function LENGTH(Phrase) calculates the length of a string Phrase.

items.prompt: Write the pseudocode statements to: store the string "The beginning is the most important part" in Phrase; calculate and output the length of the string; output the string in upper case.
items.modelAnswer:
Phrase <- "The beginning is the most important part"
OUTPUT LENGTH(Phrase)
OUTPUT UCASE(Phrase)
Marks for: storing the string in Phrase, using LENGTH, using UCASE, and outputting both results.

steps.label: Exam Question: Find the W
steps.content:
Exam Question: Find the W

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must P be changed to upper case before the search?Show the answer

Q is a capital W. "The world" has a small w, and = sees w and W as different, so without UCASE the W is never found.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/22, June 2023, Question 11(c). P stores the string "The world". Q stores the character 'W'. An algorithm converts P to upper case, then finds the position of Q in the string P (the first character in this string is in position 1), and stores it in the variable Position.

P <- "The world"
Q <- 'W'
P <- UCASE(P)
Total: 1 mark

Exam Question: Make a Username

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the system add a random number to each username?Show the answer

Two people can have the same letters, such as Mai Han and Mo Hann. The number makes each username different.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/21, June 2026, Question 5(b). A system makes usernames. It takes the first letter of the first name and the first two letters of the last name, converts all the letters to upper case, and adds a random number: Muhammed Hann gets MHA492. The last name is input into the variable LastName.

Total: 3 marks
